opening.text: Open with the operating question. At the end of today, how accurately can we forecast ERCOT’s total demand for every hour tomorrow? Introduce the four team members. The four speaking blocks cover data and EDA, the LSTM, classical forecasting, and numerical optimization.

intro.what: We forecast each of the next 24 hourly electricity loads for the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), using observed system load from January 2018 through November 4, 2026. At the end of day d, each model forecasts the 24 hourly loads of day d + 1. Two questions: which model predicts most accurately on identical out-of-time hours, and how do the optimizers compare on a shared Ridge objective and a shared neural network?

stops.title: Cleaning the Data
stops.headline: 619,968 zone rows reduce to 77,496 system hours, split by year
stops.sub: The raw file repeats ERCOT system demand on all eight weather-zone rows for each hour; the audit found a 0 MW spread across zones. Keeping one row per timestamp and daylight-saving flag leaves one target per physical hour. Fitting used 2018–2023, selection used 2024–2025, and scoring used 2026 through November 4.
stops.say: The raw file repeats system demand on all eight zone rows, so 619,968 rows reduce to 77,496 hours, split by year into train, validation, and test.
stats: Matched 2026 test hours for every model
callouts: Forecast timing
At the end of day d, each model forecasts the 24 hourly loads of day d + 1 from historical loads and calendar information. Observed target-day weather is excluded.

details.label: Details: split sizes and data-issue treatments (report Tables 2–3)

rows: Both records kept in the hourly audit; neural inputs average the repeated hour for a fixed 24-slot day.
Neural pipelines interpolate the missing slot; Ridge/SVR excludes affected days and incomplete lag profiles.
No test target for that day; the LSTM fills input history with the same hour one week earlier.
Imputed with training-period medians; target-day observed weather is excluded from forecast features.

notes.text:
We predict all 24 hourly loads at the forecast origin. The main forecasts use information available at that origin, including deterministic calendars. The final comparison is based on the intersection of the models’ test timestamps. Define MAE as average absolute error and RMSE as a measure that weights large errors more heavily.

Each physical hour appears eight times, once per weather zone, but the system target is identical on those rows. We verified zero cross-zone spread for the repeated system target and deduplicated using timestamp and daylight-saving flag. The raw table has 274 missing weather cells across 67 records. The neural pipelines use a fixed 24-slot daily profile, while the classical models require complete target and lag days. October 30 has no observed target. Because the pipelines handle transition days and gaps differently, we aligned their forecasts after predicting. We fit scaling using training data only and kept the year blocks chronological.

Explain the treatment of repeated and missing local hours. The raw audit retains both physical fall-back hours. The daily models regularize fixed 24-slot profiles. The October 30 gap has no observed target. The common test cohort is chosen by timestamp to support a fair model comparison.

stops.title: Load Patterns
stops.headline: Average load rose 30.3% from training to test; the daily mean swings 15.28 GW
stops.sub: Mean load was 45.81 GW in 2018–2023, 54.13 GW in 2024–2025, and 59.69 GW in 2026. The average day has its low near 03:00 (40.87 GW) and its high near 17:00 (56.15 GW). Seasonal peaks and the shift in load level motivate lag and calendar inputs.
stops.say: Average load rose 30.3% from training to test, and the average day swings about 15 gigawatts between 3 AM and 5 PM.

Flagged for 168 system hours, February 14–20, 2021, inside the training period. The primary LSTM excluded 21 training windows that intersect it.

notes.text:
Point out the rise in weekly demand and the typical overnight trough and late-afternoon crest. The shaded bands are validation and test. The mean moved from 45.81 GW in training to 59.69 GW in 2026. Use the next slide to look more closely at the seasonal pattern.

Compare March and August on the same vertical scale. The monthly means pool years and the November 2026 window ends early. The patterns help explain why season indicators and recent load levels are included. Hand off to Speaker 2 to discuss the LSTM.

stops.title: Ridge vs. RBF-SVR
stops.headline: RBF-SVR beat Ridge on 2024–2025 validation; Ridge beat RBF-SVR on the 2026 test
stops.sub: Both models use the same 12 inputs per hour: same-hour load one day and one week earlier, summaries of the previous day, and calendar encodings. Ridge fits an L2-penalized linear relationship; the RBF kernel can represent nonlinear relationships. Settings were selected by validation MAE.
stops.say: With the same 12 inputs, RBF-SVR was 41 megawatts better on validation, but Ridge was 57 megawatts better on the 2026 test.

charts.title: Measured load and both classical forecasts, first 168 test hours

callouts: Ranking did not carry over
The validation ranking did not carry over to test. The 2026 maximum (91.13 GW) is above the training maximum (85.46 GW).

details.label: Details: the 12 inputs, Ridge α search, and 12 SVR settings (report Tables 5–6)

charts.title: Ridge validation MAE by regularization α

rows: Previous day mean, maximum, and minimum load
Sine/cosine of hour, weekday, month; weekend flag

notes.text:
List the main predictors: the same hour yesterday and last week, previous-day load summaries, and cyclical hour, weekday and month. The Ridge model estimates a regularized linear relationship. The SVR uses an RBF kernel and standardizes the target for fitting. The plot shows measured and forecast demand at the beginning of the test period. Both pick up the broad recurring shape, while some turning points and peaks remain difficult. The view is an example; we evaluate model ranking on all common hours.

Explain that alpha sets the Ridge penalty; its best value on validation was 0.1, but the low-alpha portion of the grid is nearly flat. For SVR, C controls the penalty on deviations, epsilon the insensitive zone, and gamma the kernel scale. The SVR validation advantage was around 41 MW, yet the chronological test ranked Ridge around 57 MW ahead. The largest change in this comparison is across time periods, so validation ranking alone would have given the opposite result.

stops.title: LSTM Ensemble
stops.headline: The 3-seed LSTM ensemble reads 14 days of history and had the lowest 2026 MAE: 1,691.65 MW
stops.sub: Each input holds 14 daily steps of 24 hourly loads plus calendar features, with load divided by the preceding seven-day average. Two 64-unit LSTM layers feed a head that predicts all 24 hours jointly. Forecasts from seeds 42, 7, and 2026 are averaged in MW before scoring.
stops.say: The LSTM reads 14 days of hourly history, predicts all 24 hours together, and averages three seeds; its 2026 MAE was 29.3% lower than the previous-day baseline.
flow: Divide each 14-day window of hourly load by the preceding seven-day average.
Recurrent stack; the head adds target-day calendar and recent load level.
Predict 24 hours jointly, convert back to MW, average seeds 42, 7, 2026.
callouts: Ensemble vs. single seeds
Validation MAE: seed 42 1,645.63, seed 7 1,622.42, seed 2026 1,640.39 MW. Averaged forecast: 1,621.87 MW.

details.label: Details: checkpoints, Uri and weather checks (report Table 7, Figure 6)

charts.title: Original LSTM training diagnostics (objective, validation loss, gradient norm, learning rate)

rows: Hindsight upper bound; unavailable at issuance, excluded from the comparison

notes.text:
Each timestep represents a day, so the recurrent stack reads one two-week context rather than 336 individual hourly timesteps. The 24-load vector describes the shape of the day. Day-of-week and other calendar features help the model distinguish working days and weekends. A recent seven-day average gives the network a changing demand scale. The final recurrent state and target-day calendar feed a 128-unit forecast head. Each seed model has 70,424 parameters. Average predictions in MW before evaluating the ensemble.

Read the four training diagnostics left to right. The objective and validation loss decline early, then improve more slowly. The logged gradient norms are measured before clipping. The plateau scheduler reduces the learning rate when the validation objective stops improving.

Show the variation in epoch and MAE across the three runs. The 3-seed forecast is scored after averaging the hourly predictions, which is why its MAE is different from the mean of individual MAEs. Describe the learning-rate plateau schedule and early stopping. The core fit excluded 21 training windows that touched the Uri interval. Keeping them changed validation MAE by 0.26 MW on seed 42. The optional run with observed future weather is a hindsight upper bound and is outside the deployable comparison shown here.

These sensitivity rows use seed 42. Including storm windows barely changes MAE in this run. The weather experiment includes observations that would be unavailable at issuance, giving a hindsight comparison rather than an operational result.

Indicate the hour axis and explain that each line value averages 301 errors at that local hour. For the LSTM, MAE is about 556 MW at 00:00 and 2,892 MW at 17:00. The later forecast hours are harder on this cohort. The previous-day baseline has 2,393.23 MW aggregate MAE, compared with 1,691.65 for the ensemble. The LSTM also has lower daily MAE than Ridge on 214 of 301 matched dates. This is descriptive; we do not assume the daily results are independent. Hand off to Speaker 3 to discuss the classical models and the comparison table.

stops.title: Ridge Solvers
stops.headline: On the same Ridge objective, conjugate gradient reached tolerance in 13 iterations; Armijo needed 4,749
stops.sub: All three solvers minimize the same strictly convex quadratic from zero and stop when the gradient norm falls to 10⁻⁸ of its starting value, or at 10,000 iterations. Fixed-step gradient descent uses step 1/L; Armijo tests step 1.0 and halves it as needed; linear conjugate gradient solves the normal equations.
stops.say: On the same Ridge objective, conjugate gradient converged in 13 iterations, Armijo in 4,749, and fixed-step descent hit the 10,000 cap; CG's median time was 292× shorter than Armijo's.
stats: Conjugate gradient (292× less time than Armijo)
Fixed-step GD (cap reached; up to 0.168 MW from reference)

charts.title: Ridge objective gap by iteration (same objective, same start)

callouts: Same solution
CG and Armijo validation predictions agreed with the Cholesky reference within 0.014 MW; both had validation MAE ≈ 2,307.95 MW.
Iteration bound
In exact arithmetic, linear CG terminates in at most d iterations on a d-dimensional quadratic [Nocedal & Wright]. Here d = 12.

details.label: Details: objective and solver table (report Table 11)
details.formula: f(w) = (‖Xw − y‖² + α‖w‖²) / (2n),   α = 0.1;   stop when ‖∇f‖ ≤ 10⁻⁸ ‖∇f₀‖ or 10,000 iterations

notes.text:
Define the Ridge objective and the relative gradient tolerance. The intercept is recovered from centered data. Solver comparisons use the same objective, the same zero start, and a Cholesky Ridge reference.

The Ridge objective is squared residuals plus an L2 penalty, giving a positive-definite quadratic after centering. Fixed-step descent uses one over the largest Hessian eigenvalue. Armijo starts at step one and halves until sufficient decrease holds. Conjugate gradient uses the structure of the same quadratic. It reached tolerance in 13 iterations; Armijo needed 4,749 and fixed-step descent hit 10,000. The two converged methods give essentially identical validation predictions. The comparison is about solving the objective efficiently, and the timings are specific to this implementation and hardware.

stops.title: Network Optimizers
stops.headline: On the feed-forward network, mini-batch SGD gave lower validation MAE than full-batch Armijo for all three seeds
stops.sub: Both methods started from identical weights and ran 100 passes through the 2,184 training days of a 67 → 64 → 24 ReLU network. Full-batch Armijo took one gradient step per pass (100 total); mini-batch SGD used shuffled batches of 32 (6,900 updates). Each kept its lowest-validation-MAE checkpoint.
stops.say: With a 100-pass budget, mini-batch SGD beat full-batch Armijo on validation for all three seeds, by 234 megawatts on average; Armijo used less optimizer time.

LSTM tuning
The best single-seed screen trial (7-day lookback) improved seed 42 by 20.85 MW; across three seeds the original configuration ranked first (1,621.87 MW).

details.label: Details: paired seeds and LSTM tuning (report Tables 13–15, 17)

notes.text:
Use the equal-pass graph to show the different learning curves. Armijo uses one full-batch update per pass and made 185 candidate objective evaluations. SGD at rate 0.03 performs 69 mini-batch updates per pass, for 6,900 across the timed run. A gradient call represents different sample counts. SGD used more optimizer time in the measured run and achieved lower forecast errors. The three-seed validation means shown are accompanied by sample standard deviations. The 14.2 percent test improvement is the matched seed-42 result; the two added seeds were assessed on validation.

Read the paired MAEs across the three seeds. These differences are computed within each matched initialization. Under equal passes, the gradient counts differ because each mini-batch is smaller than the full training set. The extra seed runs were scored on validation.

The 7-day, 64-unit trial improved seed 42’s validation MAE by 20.85 MW, but averaged predictions across three seeds reversed that ranking by roughly one megawatt. A separate batch-size sweep changed only the batch size and again favored the original. These are validation decisions. The added settings were not evaluated on 2026, and the original forecast is retained. Emphasize why reporting the unsuccessful tuning is valuable: it shows the single-seed gain was not reliable.

stops.title: 2026 Results
stops.headline: On 301 matched 2026 days, the LSTM ensemble ranked first and led second place by 94.94 MW
stops.sub: Every forecast is scored on the same 301 days and 7,224 hours. The LSTM's MAE was 29.3% lower than the previous-day baseline, 26.3% lower than Ridge, and 5.3% lower than the SGD-trained network. The ranking is the same for MAE and RMSE.
stops.say: On the same 7,224 hours, the LSTM ensemble ranked first at 1,692 megawatts MAE, the SGD-trained network second at 1,787, and Ridge and RBF-SVR fourth and fifth.

charts.title: 2026 MAE on 7,224 matched hours (lower is better)

callouts: Report conclusion
The LSTM ensemble delivered the best observed 24-hour forecast. Feature representations and training sizes differ across model families, so the ranking compares complete pipelines.

details.label: Details: MAE and RMSE for all seven forecasts (report Table 8)

notes.text:
Read the first three rows and point out that the model ranking is the same for MAE and RMSE. Both classical models beat previous-day persistence on this test set; previous-week persistence is weakest. Comparing date ranges alone can hide mismatched daylight-saving and missing-history filters. These scores use exactly the same timestamps and observed loads. The highest observed demand was 91,133.73 MW on July 22 at 17:00; the LSTM underpredicted that point by about 3.30 GW. Hand off to Speaker 4 for the solver studies and tuning.

Recap three headline results: the LSTM ranked first on forecast errors, conjugate gradient solved Ridge most efficiently, and mini-batch SGD won on validation for all three feed-forward seeds. The next slide shows where forecast error still matters.

stops.title: Peak Hours & Limits
stops.headline: All five learned forecasts were below the 91.13 GW peak, and spring had the highest error for each model
stops.sub: At the 2026 maximum (July 22, 17:00, 91,133.73 MW) the LSTM was 3,299.60 MW low, the smallest miss of the five learned forecasts. Across the year, LSTM MAE was 1,963.42 MW in March–May and 1,525.67 MW in June–August, and rose from 555.73 MW at hour 00 to 2,143.70 MW at hour 23.
stops.say: Every learned forecast came in under the 91.1 gigawatt peak, the LSTM by 3.3; spring was the hardest season for each model.

callouts: Limitations (report)

Testing covers one partial year. Preliminary 2026 results were viewed before the optimization follow-ups. Six LSTM test days absent from the Ridge/SVR export are omitted. An autoregressive benchmark and battery dispatch were outside the completed experiments.

details.label: Details: top-decile hours and peak-hour errors (report Tables 9–10)

notes.text:
At 17:00 on July 22, measured demand was 91.13 GW. Both models undershot the observed peak. SVR came closer on this hour, despite higher overall test MAE. Emphasize that this plotted day was chosen by observed maximum load.

Distinguish an average over the 723 highest observed load hours from signed error at a single peak. The highest observed demand was 91.13 GW, and every model displayed underestimated it. The LSTM had the smallest top-decile MAE among the displayed models.

Describe three additional checks. Repeat the time split at multiple origins. Use archived weather forecasts with verified issue times if they are available. Track peak magnitude and timing and signed bias as complementary diagnostics. None of these checks is part of the completed results.
